title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 140
paragraphs: Such, then, was Alexander son of Amyntas's ancestry; and when he came to Athens, sent by Mardonius, he spoke as follows: “Athenians, Mardonius speaks these words: ‘A message has come to me from the king, which says: To the Athenians I remit all the offenses they committed against me; and now, Mardonius, do this — first, give them back their own land; then let them choose another in addition to their own, whichever they wish, remaining independent; and set up all their temples again, which I burned, provided that they agree to a treaty with me.' This message having come to me, I must do so unless I am prevented by you. Now I say to you: Why are you so mad as to raise war against the king? You will neither overcome him nor be able to hold out against him forever. You saw Xerxes's host and its deeds, and you know the power now with me, so that even if you defeat us (of which you can have no real hope if you are rightly minded), another army will come many times as large. Do not, then, try to match yourselves against the king and so be both deprived of your land and forever running for your lives; but make peace with him. You have a most honorable occasion for making peace, since the king has himself set out upon this road. Agree to a league with us, then, without fraud or deceit, and remain free. These things Mardonius charged me to say to you, Athenians. For myself, I will say nothing of my goodwill toward you — you are not learning of it now for the first time. But I ask you to do as Mardonius says, since I see that you will not be able to war with Xerxes forever. If I saw that you had the ability to do that, I would never have come to you speaking these words. For the king's power is above mortal measure and his arm is very long. If, therefore, you do not make an agreement at once, when they are offering you great things as terms for a treaty — I fear for you, seeing that you dwell more on the highway than any of your allies, and are forever exposed alone to destruction, the land you hold being cut off from the rest and lying between the armies contending together. Be persuaded — for this is a matter of great consequence to you, that to you alone of the Greeks the great king remits the offenses committed and desires to become a friend.'”
